headline: High: shared web/file tooling and broad egress create default risks of leakage, prompt injection, and unsafe cross-agent actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: open-webui ingests browser/web content, MCP, and files, while Replit Agent can read/write workspace files and execute shell commands. A shared file or tool-output bridge lets attacker-controlled content from A be treated as instructions by B. The pairwise pathway is plausible in default workflows, though not proven by direct interaction evidence.
conditions: IF open-webui content is copied into Replit workspace files or prompts, B may follow injected instructions.
IF either agent parses the other's output as trusted tool instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of A outputs into B prompts.
Use a strict delimiter/template for any copied content.
Add a manual review step before B executes shell or file actions.
Restrict MCP/tool connectors to allowlisted sources only.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all cross-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: open-webui touches prompts, chat messages, documents, persistent memory, and API keys, and has broad network egress plus cloud/API connectors. Replit Agent reads and writes Repl workspace files and handles secrets. If they share files or a workspace, sensitive data can flow from A into B and then out through B's networked actions, creating a realistic exfiltration path.
conditions: IF both agents access the same file tree or mounted volume, sensitive documents or secrets can move from A to B.
IF B is given any of A's prompts, chat logs, or API keys, B can transmit them via package registries or deployments.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces.
Remove secrets from any shared directory before running either agent.
Disable outbound connectors not needed for the task.
Rotate any API keys exposed to shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: open-webui can write to local files or mounted volumes and use plugins/tools, while Replit Agent can write the Repl filesystem, execute shell, and modify git state. If both target the same repository or directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The profiles show no locking or coordination primitive, so the conflict is a default operational risk.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repo or mounted volume, file races can occur.
IF either agent commits while the other edits the same files, git history or working tree can be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Pause one agent before the other writes to the repo.
Use git branches per agent and merge manually.
Take a quick backup snapshot before concurrent edits.
requires-engineering: add file locks or an orchestrator with coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: open-webui can generate content from web/search/tool sources, and Replit Agent can act on workspace files and shell commands. If B treats A's output as authoritative, mistakes or hallucinations can cascade into code changes or deployments. The pairwise pathway exists, but B's user checkpoints and the lack of direct automation keep this below high.
conditions: IF B uses A's output as a source of truth without verification, incorrect actions can be taken.
IF A's generated facts are pasted into code or deployment steps, downstream errors can propagate.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against primary sources.
Use a checklist before any commit or deployment.
Keep A in draft-only mode for factual content.
Limit B to read-only review when consuming A outputs.
requires-engineering: add automated citation/validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: open-webui explicitly handles usage analytics, model evaluation data, persistent memory, and API keys, while Replit Agent handles source code, secrets, and deployment configuration. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into both systems, their differing cloud residency and retention practices can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not document a specific jurisdiction conflict, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in both agents, retention and access controls must be aligned.
IF EU or PHI data is entered into either cloud service without a DPA or equivalent controls, compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared prompts or files.
Confirm vendor DPAs and retention settings before use.
Delete stale chats, artifacts, and workspace copies after the task.
Store secrets only in approved secret managers.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention mappings per data class.
